dedupe_keys.name: harris county texas changes in food pantry access when floods cut the road network

description: This case study uses geographic information systems to measure how flooding changes access to food pantries in Harris County, Texas, a populous, flood-prone county with high food insecurity. The authors, researchers at Texas A&M University and the University of Florida, modelled disruptions of the road network under flooding and recalculated travel distances from neighbourhoods to food pantries; the article is free to read as an open-access copy and in PubMed Central. Coverage is Harris County, including Houston, at neighbourhood level. Access is free; the article licence is the publisher's open access terms. Caveats: only road access is modelled, pantry operating status and capacity during floods are not, and flood scenarios are modelled, not observed for each pantry. The study found that most of Harris County sees only small increases in travel distance to food pantries under extreme flooding, but some areas may lose access to pantries altogether, showing both the potential and the limits of private food assistance networks in emergency response. Simulation uses: an example of network accessibility analysis for food assistance under flood scenarios and a baseline for food distribution location models. Related records: the Houston Food Bank location-allocation model (case_study-houston-food-bank-post-disaster-location-allocation) and the Hurricane Harvey grocery research use the same region.
